items.stem: Which Redis data type is the natural fit for a ranked leaderboard ordered by score?

options.rationale: Correct: a sorted set keeps members ordered by an associated score.
A list preserves insertion order, not ranking by score.
A string stores a single value, not a ranked set.
A hash stores field-value pairs, not an ordered ranking.

items.explanation: Correct: a sorted set keeps members ordered by an associated score.

items.stem: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?

options.text: The application reads from the database, then stores the result in the cache
options.rationale: Correct: on a miss the app loads from the source and populates the cache for next time.
Redis does not query the database itself in cache-aside.
A miss is handled by falling back to the source, not failing.
A single miss does not clear the whole cache.

items.explanation: Correct: on a miss the app loads from the source and populates the cache for next time.

items.stem: Which TWO are true about Redis persistence? (Select TWO)

options.text: RDB takes point-in-time snapshots of the dataset
options.rationale: Correct: RDB produces compact point-in-time snapshots.

options.text: AOF logs write operations for replay on restart
options.rationale: Correct: AOF records write commands and replays them to rebuild state.
Redis supports persistence via RDB and AOF.

options.text: Enabling AOF guarantees zero data in memory
options.rationale: AOF concerns durability to disk; data still lives in memory.

items.explanation: Correct: RDB produces compact point-in-time snapshots.; Correct: AOF records write commands and replays them to rebuild state.
